Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: one Victoria 3 TECHNOLOGY illustration for a historical naval research tree; not a flat production-method pictogram and not a building scene.
Style/medium: restrained hand-painted volumetric game object illustration. Broad painted masses, softened brush texture, a precise readable silhouette, short restrained highlights and local shadows ON the object. Match the native Victoria 3 admiralty cloth hat, screw_frigate compact ship and steelworking painted metal objects. Natural material colors; not photoreal, glossy 3D, vector-flat, cartoon sticker, layered cut-paper, steampunk fantasy, or uniformly sepia/blue.
Composition: one coherent dominant object, centered in a square at least 1024x1024. Slightly elevated three-quarter view, complete silhouette, generous empty margins on every side. Strong large shapes that remain recognizable at 48 and 64 pixels; subordinate tiny details. No extra accessories.
Background: genuine alpha transparency outside the object and through ALL open structural gaps. All four corners fully transparent. No background color, floor, tabletop, scenic setting, black or grey matte patch, cast-shadow patch, frame, UI tile, disc, medallion or surrounding border.
Text: no readable text, letters, numbers, dates, headings, signatures, logos, labels or watermarks.
Avoid: people, hands, coats of arms, glowing outline, neon, beam effects, modern plastic or electrical equipment. Output one finished PNG icon, not a sheet or variants.
Subject: a compact early-nineteenth-century NAVAL SIGNAL FLAG HOIST, conceptually informed by Home Popham's 1803 marine vocabulary. Three broad rectangular fabric signal flags, one above another, attached along ONE taut vertical hemp halyard with a short natural rope loop at the top. The flags billow gently in the same direction, exposing nearly frontal simple geometric patterns: top flag divided into muted vermilion-red and ivory-white blocks, middle flag muted navy-blue with a broad ivory diagonal band, bottom flag muted mustard-yellow with a broad dark-red central block. These are illustrative unlettered signal patterns, NOT national flags or a claim to transcribe an exact historical coded message. The largest top flag and two slightly smaller lower flags form one coherent compact silhouette, broadly similar widths, not a long skinny pennant chain. Clearly visible fully transparent separation between flags, fabric folds painted subtly in volume, natural aged CLOTH without dirt or holes. No excessive fraying, fringe, star symbols, crosses, modern printed digits, sailors, ship, mast, semaphore arms, flag book, telescope, cannon or ornamental finial. The rope is only the integral support; no horizontal pole, yard or wooden display stand. Retain true alpha in the hanging loop and every gap. The flags are substantial painted fabric, not flat gold badges, cut-paper strips or glossy plastic.

Subject: one compact WOODEN SHIP HULL MIDSECTION CUTAWAY showing diagonal internal reinforcing riders, inspired by Seppings' improved construction around 1814 as represented in Royal Museums Greenwich model SLR2908. A short section of curved U-shaped oak hull ribs on a small integral keel, with a few dark outer planks low on the hull. Three broad curved ribs give an unmistakably boat-shaped open cradle; a pair of thick slanting timber braces cross the visible inside side wall at different angles, forming clear LARGE DIAGONAL triangles rather than just vertical framing. Show the diagonal braces prominently in front of the rib system; their visible sloping lines should survive at 48px. Warm honey-brown and dark natural oak wood with subtle brushed grain, differentiated light and dark timber faces, restrained short highlights. Slight three-quarter view reveals the inside curve, short length, squared cut ends and real structural depth. This is a single simplified construction section, not an exact engineering replica of the full museum warship. Use few thick structural members, avoid a forest of fine sticks. Open rib and brace spaces are genuinely transparent, never backed by a grey panel. No complete ship, sails, mast, rigging, artillery, dockyard, workers, deck furniture, blueprint, crate, house frame, pedestal or museum label. The keel belongs to the structure; no extra display base.

Subject: one compact EARLY RIVETED IRON BOAT HULL BOW SECTION, a short curved plated bow with an open cutaway rear showing a few simple curved forged angle-iron frames. Conceptually informed by the original Vulcan canal boat built in 1818-1819: flush edge-to-edge iron plates riveted onto overlapping INTERNAL butt straps, supported by forged angle-iron ribs. Show an unmistakably boat-shaped rounded V/U bowl, a tapered upward bow at one end and a clean open cross-section at the other. Three or four broad dark neutral-grey rolled-iron plates define the curved shell, with sparse clearly painted aligned rivet rows; avoid random decorative dots. On the open cut end show two or three thick curved iron ribs attached behind the shell and a short integral keel, visually simple and large. Neutral charcoal and warm weathered-grey metal, subtle oxide-brown wear at a few joints and short ivory glints; no dominant blue chrome tint. Readable broad painted metal volumes, not a photoreal industrial CAD render. No bright red cabin, full canal barge, steam machinery, propeller, turret, armor belt, cannon, modern welded steel grid, Titanic-sized frames, drydock, scaffolding, workers or tools. This illustrates the ORIGINAL early iron hull principle, not the 1988 mild-steel museum replica as a period artifact, and not copper sheathing over timber. No wooden ribs or golden copper plates. True alpha exterior and through the open rear frame spaces; no water, solid shadow patch or display stand.
